speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In April this year, the Minister for Law delivered a Ministerial Statement on the establishment of a Public Defender's Office to deliver criminal defence aid.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Minister said that this is a significant shift in policy.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Before this, in 2015, we began directly funding CLAS.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This is the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme run by the Law Society Pro Bono Services.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In 2019, we began studying how else we could make criminal legal aid available to the vulnerable in society.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We decided that setting up a Public Defender's Office, or PDO, is the right model for Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This is a very significant move as the state is taking on a direct role of providing criminal legal aid.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Today's Bill provides for the establishment of a criminal defence aid scheme, to be administered by the PDO.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This has come after intense consultations – at least 10 consultations with the Law Society and Criminal Bar over the last two years.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: I will now sketch out the reasons for setting up the PDO and explain the shift in our philosophy towards criminal legal aid.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The previous view taken, in light of the developments in Singapore then, was that the state should not be paying to defend accused persons.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Before accused persons are charged, there would have been thorough investigations done by the Police.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Attorney-General's Chambers (AGC) would also have reviewed decisions to charge.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: However, this would have to be balanced against the need for accused persons not to be denied representation, in their defence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: For a long time, the balance has been struck against providing representation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This is a question of judgement and our view is that the right balance was struck at that time.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: However, in today's Singapore, we think that the balance has shifted.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: With this, we need to consider, first, who we should help.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These households are around the 25th percentile of resident households by income.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Second, we need to consider how our existing model of criminal legal aid can be improved.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Today, criminal legal aid is provided through CLAS, which we began funding in 2015.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: However, the number of cases that CLAS could handle, is dependent on the support from the Bar.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Whereas if the Government steps in, the assurance level for the provision of legal support can be higher.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Our assessment is that the Government should provide more assistance to help needy Singaporeans who cannot afford legal representation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Hence, we will be establishing the PDO to help such accused persons.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This is a significant move as it will institutionalise public defence within our criminal justice system.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The PDO will have its own full-time officers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This will allow us to deliver timely and higher quality representation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The PDO will also help to build up the capabilities of the criminal bar.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Minister for Law had spoken at length during his Ministerial Statement about the experiences of other jurisdictions with Public Defender Schemes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This was due to continual increases in lawyers' fees of around 4% to 10% every year.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: He also shared other examples of abuse from various jurisdictions and how these strained the public purse, and led to cuts in funding.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: For instance, some asset-rich individuals managed to find ways to meet the eligibility criteria.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These legal aid recipients would show up in Rolls Royces and other fancy cars, which they said were not theirs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Thus, while we press ahead to establish our own PDO, we must be careful to avoid the challenges of escalating costs and abuse by accused persons who can afford representation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It is important to learn from others' experiences and avoid making the same mistakes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We are determined not to run down their routes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This includes instituting various safeguards into the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: That is why we are moving this Bill – to provide us with a strong governance framework, with legal backing, for the PDO.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We will set up the PDO as a department under MinLaw.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This enables better oversight of criminal defence aid by MinLaw.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The PDO will be helmed by a Chief Public Defender or Chief PD.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: He will report to the Permanent Secretary and Minister for Law.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Chief PD will maintain operational and professional independence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Chief PD and his team will exercise their discretion in deciding whether to grant aid or not, by carefully examining the merits of each legal aid application.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: They will also be able to exercise their professional independence when providing representation and advice to persons granted legal aid.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Second, to ensure that only deserving applicants receive aid, all applications for criminal defence aid will be subjected to robust means and merits tests.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These tests are our key gatekeepers to ensure that aid is given to those who truly need it.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: There may still be applicants who try to game the system to get aid.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: For example, they may not be eligible for aid, but lie about their means or make false declarations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: There will be criminal penalties to deter such behaviour.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Third, to keep our costs in check while ensuring quality representation, frameworks will be put in place for the PDO to ensure costs continue to remain sustainable.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This will allow us to budget and let us know what the overall cost will be.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: I will emphasise again what the Minister for Law mentioned in his Ministerial Statement.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: If there is no careful control of the cost initially, it would be difficult to bring it back down later.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We will build up the capability and credibility of the PDO to command the trust and respect of Singaporeans, the legal fraternity and the accused persons we serve.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We have to learn from the examples of other Public Defender Schemes overseas and take pre-emptive steps to make sure we do not face the same issues.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This is not going to be easy, as there will be demand for legal representation and we would have to be careful about this.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Having set out the broader policy considerations behind the PDO, I will now turn to the provisions in the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: There are four key areas: first, the appointment of the PDO's officers; second, the scope of aid, called criminal defence aid in the Bill; third, the administration of criminal defence aid; and fourth, the penalty framework.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: First, the appointment of the Chief PD and other officers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Bill provides for the appointment by the Minister of a Chief PD, Deputy Chief Public Defenders and Assistant Chief Public Defenders.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Chief PD can also appoint qualified and experienced persons as Public Defenders to assist him or her.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The officers of the PDO, or PD Officers, will have the right to appear and plead in the Courts, and can therefore represent aided accused persons.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Just like a Deputy Public Prosecutor, a PD Officer is expected to assist the Court in coming to a correct decision in respect of guilt or sentence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Bill also includes related amendments to the Evidence Act and the Legal Profession Act, to bring PD Officers under the provisions of both Acts, where relevant.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The related amendments to the Legal Profession Act ensure that the PD Officers have the standing to advise and represent accused persons in criminal proceedings and subject PD Officers, as officers of the Court, to the disciplinary framework administered by the Supreme Court.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This disciplinary framework currently applies to officers under the Judicial and Legal Service Schemes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This gives the public confidence that PD Officers are subject to the same checks and balances as Judicial and Legal Service Officers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The related amendments to the Evidence Act are for the purpose of extending statutory protection to PD Officers, in respect of professional communications with an advocate or a solicitor.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: An SCPR is therefore not eligible for aid if he or she is only under investigation for such an offence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The scope of criminal defence aid also covers criminal appeals or criminal applications arising from criminal proceedings instituted against the applicant.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Second, offences that are generally regulatory in nature.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This refers to minor offences for which the accused person is served	a notice to attend Court or a summons by an officer of a statutory body or Government agency.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This exclusion is not intended to extend to criminal offences that are dealt with by law enforcement agencies such as the Singapore Police Force, Central Narcotics Bureau and Corrupt Practices Investigation Bureau.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This ensures that criminal defence aid is only given in respect of proceedings for serious offences as opposed to minor traffic offences or offences brought under departmental summonses such as littering and failure to file income tax returns.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Third, offences under 10 Acts whose main purpose is to deter behaviours that bring about negative externalities to society.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These offences cover gambling and betting, organised and syndicated crime, and terrorism.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Criminal defence aid will only be given for state prosecutions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: If an applicant for aid does not qualify because his offences are excluded, his application falls outside of the Bill but it does not mean that he cannot obtain legal aid elsewhere.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: If there are such applications that may deserve aid due to their particular circumstances, the applicant may apply instead to the Law Society Pro Bono Services, or LSPBS, for consideration.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Bill provides for criminal defence aid to be given to accused persons who face multiple charges before the same Court in respect of offences, some of which are excluded offences.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The PDO can represent such accused persons if he or she passes the means and merits test for the offences that are not excluded.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This will allow the PDO to effectively represent the aided person when all his charges are dealt with in the same Court.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: As mentioned earlier, all applications for criminal defence aid will be subjected to rigorous means and merits tests.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These tests ensure that only deserving and needy applicants receive aid.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Chief PD can also refer applications that pass the means and merits tests to other organisations to provide legal aid rather than assign the case to a PD officer.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: And the PDO will co-deliver aid with CLAS.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The exact means test criteria will be laid out in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It will comprise two components: income and wealth.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This is a significant move to ensure we cover more needy applicants who would otherwise struggle to pay for a lawyer at these income thresholds.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The wealth component looks at an applicant's savings, assets and investments.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Even if an applicant does not satisfy the means test criteria, the Minister can direct the Chief PD to grant aid if the Minister is of the opinion that it is just and proper to do so.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This gives leeway to provide aid to those who do not satisfy the means test criteria but are unable to afford legal services due to extenuating circumstances.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: For example, an applicant may be battling an illness or may have to care for an incapacitated family member.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We will consider all relevant circumstances in the grant of aid.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: For the merits test, aid can be granted where the applicant requires legal representation to plead guilty or there are reasonable grounds for defence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In appeal cases, aid can be granted where there are merits to the appeal brought by the applicant or in defending the appeal brought by the prosecution.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The merits test will be administered in two ways.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: For expediency, the Chief PD will decide on the merits to an application in respect of offences or class of offences that carry lesser penalties.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The merits to an application in respect of offences or class of offences that carry heavier penalties will be decided by a board comprising the Chief PD and at least two private solicitors.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This ensures that applications with more severe offences will be subject to greater deliberation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Solicitors on the board will also provide a diverse and independent point of view on the application and enhance public confidence in the merits test assessment.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This classification will be provided in the subsidiary legislation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Chief PD can also refuse aid if he considers that it is not appropriate in the circumstances of the applicant's case to grant aid.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This could include cases where the applicant may not benefit much from legal representation, such as those with established sentencing frameworks.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Where the Chief PD decides not to grant aid, the Minister is empowered to authorise the Chief PD to grant aid in the interest of justice.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Examples are those in remand or who are minors.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Such applicants can be issued with a provisional grant of aid if they are likely to pass the means and merits tests.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This ensures that no deserving applicant will be denied aid while waiting for the means and merits tests to be completed.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: To prevent wastage of resources, the Chief PD can refuse to consider repeat applications for the same matter unless there is a change in circumstances.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This ensures that resources are optimally allocated to deserving cases.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The PDO will only represent one accused person in proceedings involving multiple co-accused persons, if more than one party qualifies for aid.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This is to prevent any potential or perceived conflicts of interest where the co-accused persons have inconsistent defences.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Chief PD will have the discretion to decide which accused person will be represented by the PDO.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The other co-accused persons may be referred to CLAS.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Applicants will be required to co-pay the costs of legal aid.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The less they have, the less they pay and vice versa.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Those with very little savings and investments may even pay nothing.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This ensures that applicants contribute towards their defence and do not abuse the system.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This is no different from the current approach by CLAS and the Legal Aid Bureau for civil legal aid.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The co-payments may be provided in a lump sum or by instalments.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Chief PD will have the discretion to reduce, waive or refund any such contributions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In future, the PDO will adopt a hybrid model of managing cases in-house while outsourcing some others to the private sector.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: To cater for this, the Bill includes provisions for the appointment of one or more panels of solicitors to act for aided accused persons and for the solicitors to be paid fees.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The fees payable to a solicitor will be agreed on between the Chief PD and the solicitor based on considerations that include: the complexity or novelty of the issues involved in the case; as well as the skill and specialised knowledge required of; and time and labour expended by, the solicitor.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This includes making false or misleading statements in the application, failing to make full and frank disclosure about one's means or failing to inform about changes in one's means or other circumstances that would render an applicant ineligible for aid.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Bill also provides for the Court to order costs against a person who: (a)	obtained aid through fraud or misrepresentation; or (b)	acted improperly in defending or contesting any proceedings or in the conduct of those proceedings.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In my speech during the debate, I said that our society has and continues to be strongly anchored in the rule of law.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I observed that since Independence, great strides have been taken to improve the administration of justice in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I acknowledged, however, that further work needs to be done in our quest to ensure that such administration is accessible to all.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This arena will always be a work in progress.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For new proposals to be implemented, there is a need to strike a balance between the interests of the crime victims, accused persons, members of public and effective marshalling of public resources.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is to enhance access to justice for these vulnerable persons.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I believe this is a development that hon Members from both sides of the House would welcome.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is also noteworthy that the Government's position on the issue of providing legal aid to accused persons in	criminal proceedings has evolved over the years.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Twenty-seven years ago in this House, the hon Minister for Law then, Prof S Jayakumar, stated in unambiguous terms the Government's original position that it was incongruous for the state to fund the legal defence of accused persons.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He said that accused persons are only brought to book after a thorough and careful process.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He went on to state, "Why are they prosecuted?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They are prosecuted in the public interest and the state expends these monies in the public interest and in order to protect the law-abiding majority...

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is incongruous and inconsistent that public funds should be used to defend an accused person which the state has decided ought to be charged in Court and use public funds at the same time to get him off.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The exception is where life is involved and for capital cases, counsel is assigned." The Government's position changed in November 2013 when it announced its decision to fund the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme, a volunteer scheme run by the Law Society since 1985 to help indigent accused persons.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: At the launch of this funding programme in 2015, the hon Minister for Law stated that, "This represents a significant shift in the Government's philosophy." But there remained the issue of the model.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In 2006, the hon Minister Indranee Rajah, then a backbencher, put it pithily.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: She said in this House, "It just seems a little odd that for something as serious as a criminal charge, these persons would actually have to defend on a volunteer scheme." She then called on the Government to extend legal aid to cover criminal matters as well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We agree that on the point of fairness, access to justice cannot be denied to those who cannot afford it.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Can I ask the hon Senior Parliamentary Secretary for some data relating to accused persons who have legal representation and those without as a percentage of the cases prosecuted by the state, how many have legal representation and how many do not?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Where the accused persons claim trial, what is the percentage of success in terms of acquittal for those who have legal representation and those who do not?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am aware that this is a crude piece of data.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The difference in the acquittal rates is a function of many factors, of course, but one wonders to what extent this is due to the lack of a professional defence presented for some of these cases.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In any case, we should have this data as a point of comparison and to revisit this after the PDO has had time to run once this Bill is passed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Government will then be able to gauge what other considerations that it may have to monitor compliance with the policy objectives of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In addition to the duty to ensure access, the Government also has a corresponding duty, to maintain fiscal prudence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The basic point Prof Jayakumar made about the need to ensure fiscal sustainability when committing public resources is something we must continue to bear in mind in structuring this new office of the PDO.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is a cost that we are collectively prepared to incur in priority to other needs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As responsible Members of Parliament, therefore, we will have to bear this commitment in mind when we make a case for our Government to commit further public funds in other areas.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For us to ensure that indigent accused persons are provided with good quality representation in criminal proceedings, we need two things: first, adequate resources; and second, competent Public Defenders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Dealing with the second issue first, may I ask what steps are or will be taken to ensure that the Public Defenders consistently provide a good quality representation to indigent persons?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would also like to offer several suggestions on this matter.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, in my research, I have come across models in other countries where committees consisting of independent and eminent legal experts are set up with a view to regularly audit the work of the Public Defenders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I wonder if the hon Senior Parliamentary Secretary is minded to follow suit.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, in some countries, the PDO publishes annual reports providing information on its key performance indicators.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In fact, this is mandated in some pieces of legislation that provided for the set-up of the equivalent of the PDO.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I recommend that this practice be followed too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Turning to adequate resources, the hon Minister for Law in his April 2022 speech cautioned against following the examples in several countries where escalating costs eventually had the effect of undermining the very objective of setting up the PDO in the first place.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We need to strive to strike an appropriate balance.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: At the 35th percentile, these households would basically have little excess income that can be used for payment of legal fees.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What we need to ensure is that PDO is adequately staffed to ensure that it can handle the expected volume of cases that will be generated.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is also another aspect of providing other defence resources which I wish to touch on.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Regularly, in criminal cases, there is a need to procure public documents which are ordinarily subject to payment under the Fees Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Examples include the First Information Report, Traffic Accident Reports and cautioned statements of the accused.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is also a need to procure expert evidence such as medical opinion, handwriting expert opinion and so on.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In particular, one issue I am concerned about is where the Government has provided resources to the Prosecution, say in form of a psychiatrist, from IMH or the College of Psychiatrists, to opine on the state of mind of the accused.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Would the Government be willing to share similar resources with the PDO?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It seems to me that waiver of fees and sharing of resources will have the salutary effect of bringing down the costs of defending the accused.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I therefore, would like to encourage the Government to explore this idea.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One practical point which I wish to offer is whether the Prosecution and PDO can explore, in appropriate cases, the joint appointment of experts that will bind both sides.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This trend is already being promoted in the Civil Courts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One concern I have though involves the issue of timing.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Usually, the Prosecution may have already dealt with these issues even before an indigent person is charged in Court.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, the indigent accused person may only be entitled to criminal defence aid from the PDO after being charged in Court.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In other words, there may not be an opportunity to make a joint appointment in the circumstances I outlined.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It seems to me that having the PDO involved earlier in certain cases may allow for better cost management.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I seek the hon Senior Parliamentary Secretary's views on this.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In clause 8(1), it is provided, amongst others, that a grant of aid may be issued in respect of any "criminal proceedings" instituted in respect of an offence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, what constitutes "criminal proceedings" is not specifically defined.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As a matter of statutory interpretation, it should be interpreted in a manner that promotes the aims of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Potentially, this may also include proceedings involving military offences in the Subordinate Military Courts and the Military Court of Appeal set up under parts 5 and 7 of the Singapore Armed Forces Act 1972.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It may also potentially include proceedings under part 7 of the Industrial Relations Act 1960 for contempt in the Industrial Arbitration Court set up under the same Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As can be imagined, the PD can face formidable challenges when he is instructed to act for an accused with mental illness.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He needs to ensure that he is authorised to act for the accused.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He needs to take instructions on the conduct of the case as well as provide advice.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The question is who should be the proxy for the accused in these circumstances?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In other jurisdictions, there are specific provisions that will enable a PD to be empowered to act for and take instructions on behalf of a mentally ill accused through a Court appointed guardian or intermediary.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: From my perusal of the Bill, although there are provisions dealing with applications for the grant of criminal defence aid to a minor, there are no similar provisions dealing with persons with mental issues.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I take it that it is proposed that the prescribed circumstances are to be provided in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Of the two functions, we need to see that the prosecution of persons who do harm as mainly driven by the pursuit of public goods such as safety, peace and security.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They are driven by the fairness of due process, which includes the exercise of mercy and compassion – a point that the hon Senior Parliamentary Secretary made admirably in her speech.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This Motion was filed in the wake of the case involving, Ms Parti Liyani, a domestic worker, whose theft convictions had been overturned on appeal in the High Court.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Though that case was the trigger for the debate, the Motion was filed on a wider basis, extending to how the criminal justice system operated against those who could not afford legal representation.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It was notable that there was substantial agreement between the Government and the Workers' Party on the need for some enhancements.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, the Government emphasised that it needed to decide on what specific changes to implement and how to pay for them.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The fact that the Government is tabling this Bill today shows that it has squared that circle, as far as enhancing of criminal legal aid is concerned.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My party colleague, Ms He Ting Ru will speak more about this later.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This Bill is in my view overdue, but as they say, better late than never.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In putting forward this Bill, the Government is recognising that fair play is fundamental to justice; so fundamental, that part of the annual national Budget should rightly be set aside for this purpose.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Nobody should question the principle behind this Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party has over the years spoken about the importance of justice for all and legal aid in criminal cases.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It was said that there was a contradiction in it funding both the prosecution and the defence.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It was the Law Society who stepped up to offer pro bono representation in non-capital cases around 30 years ago through the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme, or CLAS, on limited resources.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: CLAS was in my view the most morally uplifting project embarked on by the Law Society at the time.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Those of us involved in the early days of it in one way or another, look back with pride to see how far CLAS has come from its humble beginnings.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Over the years, the Government also evolved its position and from around 2015, started providing funding to CLAS.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This Government support has been critical to the sustainability and enhancement of CLAS.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Today, there are many lawyers, providing pro bono services under CLAS, conscious of their public duty and committed to obtaining the best outcome for their clients.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That said, it is quite clear to me that the current CLAS scheme for criminal legal aid does not adequately cover cases of need.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In my view, there are three main limiting factors, whether a case is: which is covered by the scheme or not; how poor one must be to qualify for aid, also known as the means test; and how strong one's case needs to be, also known as the merits test.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It would be important to understand how the PD scheme will widen the net to provide legal aid to more people.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First on the coverage of the PD scheme.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It should be noted that only citizens and permanent residents will be covered.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Although foreigners could well need legal aid, I accept this scoping due to the need to watch the budget, especially at this initial stage.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The scheme also does not cover a list of offences in the Schedule to the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Ten statutes are totally excluded as they relate to behaviours that should be deterred, for example, terrorist activities and gambling.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There is also a partial exclusion under 36 Acts if the accused is brought to Court by way of a notice to attend Court or a summons.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For these partially excluded Acts, this will mean that the more serious offences where the accused is brought to Court upon arrest or bail will still fall within the PDO's coverage for aid.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I think this is a sensible compromise to strike.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Going forward, this will mean, for instance, that persons facing more serious charges under the Road Traffic Act may be able to obtain criminal legal aid, which is currently totally excluded under the CLAS scheme.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is good to note the move to cover about 10% more of the population.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: According to clause 12 of the Bill, there will be two different baskets of cases to be assessed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The first basket are offences which are prescribed where the Chief Public Defender can decide whether the case has merits.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The second basket involves offences which are not prescribed, in which case, the decision on whether the case has merit will not be made by the Chief PD alone but will be made by a board consisting of the Chief PD and at least two lawyers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It would appear that cases involving prescribed offence would be approved on a faster track while those involving non-prescribed offences needed more consideration.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Earlier, the Senior Parliamentary Secretary touched on this matter and if I heard her correctly, she said that more serious offences needed more consideration.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Does it mean that offences such as furnishing false information to public servants will apply, such that witnesses who lie to the Public Defenders may be prosecuted under the Penal Code?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It would seem to be somewhat anomalous if that were the case since private defence counsel have no such powers when people lie to them.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Next, on the Minister's residual power to order aid.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This will be where the Minister considers it in the interests of justice that aid be given or where the applicant does not satisfy the means test, that it is still just and proper to grant aid.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Is the intention to use this provision only in exceptional situations?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, in April, I had asked the Minister whether the Legal Aid Scheme in Capital Cases (LASCO) administered by the Supreme Court would be brought within the PDO scheme.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Minister had then replied that it would be considered.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In the course of my work as a lawyer, I find that many accused persons struggle to understand the legal process whenever they are faced with a criminal charge.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Many times, they are not given a copy of the charge sheet and do not know what is the exact allegation being made against them.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They do not understand the concept of bail and sometimes, they just want to plead guilty without understanding the consequence of a criminal conviction.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In fact, a few of my clients had informed me that when they are charged at the Police station, it is the Police investigator who advised them on the legal process and what to expect when they attend Court.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Sometimes, the Investigation Officer informed them that if they plead guilty, the Police will ask for a lighter sentence from the Court.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Allow me to quote from a speech made in Parliament in February 2013 by my former Parliamentary colleague and the current the Deputy Attorney-General, Mr Hri Kumar.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: He said, "It is not the Government's role simply to arrest, try and jail.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Government's role is to ensure the rights of all citizens are protected and that includes making sure that those who are accused have a fair hearing.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Its KPI should not be the number of successful prosecutions, but rather that in every case, a fair and just result was achieved." He continued, "There have been cases of accused persons seeking what they consider to be the easier path – pleading guilty to an offence they did not commit simply because they cannot afford the cost of a trial.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And whenever we have cases of wrong convictions, it is a blight on our legal process and the administration of justice.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And there is no higher cost than the indelible stain of a wrong conviction, particularly, where the cause is one of lack of resources." Sir, I agree with Mr Hri Kumar's views.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I also appreciate Minister Indranee Rajah's response to Mr Kumar's speech where she stated that, "The Government's KPI is not convictions.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The Government's KPI must be and always has been justice." Ms Indranee had then replied that the Government had received suggestions about a possible Public Defender's Scheme and the Government is reviewing the suggestion.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I wish to commend the Government for their funding support for the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme (CLAS) which had given various degree of assistance to persons charged with criminal offences and who require legal advice on criminal matters.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Although it had taken some nine years since Minister Indranee's speech, I am glad that this Bill has finally been tabled in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Can the Senior Parliamentary Secretary clarify whether this requirement would expose the solicitor to allegation of breaching his professional duty to the accused person?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For example, if the solicitor obtains privileged information about the guilt of an accused person, does he have an obligation to inform or disclose to the CPD or can he seek a discharge as the solicitor if the accused person refuses to take his advice to plead guilty?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Can the Senior Parliamentary Secretary clarify whether such a solicitor can still act in a personal capacity if the accused person wants him to continue outside the Public Defender's scheme?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For example, if a solicitor insists on making frivolous applications to Court and is eventually removed from the panel, can he continue to act as a solicitor for the accused person and continue with such frivolous applications?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Clause 6 of the Bill provides for the fees payable to the solicitor to be agreed.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Can the Senior Parliamentary Secretary give an indication as to how fees can be agreed upon because it is difficult for a solicitor to determine his fees without knowing whether such a trial would drag for many days or even months?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Or would the legal fees be determined after the trial is completed?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Can the Senior Parliamentary Secretary provide greater clarity as to the timeframe for such aid to be granted?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In practice, most accused persons have very little time to respond when they are charged in Court.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Frequently, the Court allows the accused person one to two weeks to engage a lawyer before going back to Court for the next mention.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Would the Chief PD be able to assess whether an applicant would meet the criteria for criminal defence aid within two weeks?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In a situation where an accused is in remand, the Senior Parliamentary Secretary has said that the family member can apply for criminal defence aid on his behalf.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: How much time would be required before the Chief PD can assess the application for criminal defence aid if this person is in remand?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The solicitor would presumably have to visit the accused in remand to determine reasonable grounds for defending.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Would the State Court allow an accused person a longer period of time to engage counsel if the person in remand is applying for aid?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Regarding the means test referred to at clause 12(1), how does the Chief PD ensure that a rich applicant does not hide his income and assets so that he can receive the criminal defence aid?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Would the Chief PD investigate the declared sources of income and assets or would the Chief PD simply rely on the declaration made by the applicant?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I believe this point was previously made by Minister Shanmugam in Parliament that the state should not finance the criminal defence aid of a rich applicant.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Supposing there are three to four persons who are youth or juveniles who are accused of rioting and all deny responsibility for the offence, why should the Chief PD deny criminal defence aid to more than one applicant?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Would it make any difference if the applicants seeking criminal defence aid intend to simply plead guilty?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Why not allow the Chief PD the discretion to decide instead of having a statutory bar to giving criminal aid to more than one applicant in the same proceedings?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Before I conclude, I wish to refer to the speech made by the then Minister of Law, Prof Jayakumar during the Second Reading of the Amendment Bill to the Legal Aid and Advice Act in July 1995.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: He was seeking Parliament's approval to delete Part II of the Act.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Like many other countries, we continue to work to ensure that accused persons from vulnerable backgrounds do not end up being further disadvantaged, particularly because they cannot afford to be legally represented in the criminal justice system.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is why today's Bill for the creation of the Public Defender's Office (PDO) is a cornerstone in the development of our criminal justice system and its importance cannot be overstated.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The idea of a Public Defender in some form or another is also one which has existed in many other jurisdictions for many years.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While I agree that we must exercise caution in ensuring the our own PDO does not fall into a situation seen in many other countries where clients abuse the system at both the expense of the taxpayer and adversely affects the credibility of the office, we also must not forget to take on board where public defence systems do work to bring about a stronger, more robust and credible criminal justice system and to take on board these positive lessons.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is in this spirit that I would like to raise some clarifications and questions about the Bill before us.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There is concern that although there are reasons for this exemption, this ultimately compromises the client-attorney relationship or it would be seen to be compromised by the clients who may then be reticent in providing full and frank disclosure to their solicitor.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While the Bill does make it clear about the circumstances under which such disclosure may occur, namely, when deciding whether to refuse an application for criminal defence aid, to vary or cancel a grant of aid or to determine whether there are merits to an application for criminal defence aid, would it be possible to have more explicit guidelines as to what types of privileged information may be disclosable to the CPD and to ensure that the clients either consent to such disclosure or know exactly what may be disclosed and under what circumstances such disclosure will take place.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Perhaps, to allay concerns, it could also be made explicit that any such information that is necessary to be disclosed will remain strictly confidential and not disclosed to any other third parties.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As cases such as Parti Liyani's has shown, a sizeable proportion of the more vulnerable parts of our society include Work Pass holders.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These individuals would continue to rely on the goodwill of lawyers to act pro bono if they do not have the financial resources to engage a criminal defence lawyer.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While we understand that at this early stage of setting up the PDO, it would be prudent to limit its scope until the exact expenditure is known, would the Government be considering at some point, expanding coverage to long-term residents, albeit subject to more stringent criteria?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Next, moving onto the decisions themselves, relating to whether or not an applicant is granted access to aid under the PDO, the Bill provides that the CPD has the power to issue a grant of aid to an applicant, provided he has satisfied, that they meet the requirements as outlined in clause 12.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The CPD's decision would be final, except in circumstances under clause 12(7), where the Minister may overwrite the decision.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This approach is in contrast against the case of solicitors who are excluded or removed from a panel by the CPD.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In the event that the solicitor is aggrieved by the CPD's decision, they may apply to the general division of the High Court under clause 5(2) to appeal against such a decision.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This would also further enhance public confidence in the office.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This appeal process could take on the form of an appeals panel of solicitors to review the decision.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Moving on to a more general point about the criminal legal landscape in general and the impact that the PDO would have on it, part of the concern about the formation of the PDO was that this would adversely affect the livelihoods of current criminal defence practitioners.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I do not believe this should be the case, however, as the PDO has been primarily designed to expand legal representation to accused persons who do not currently have the means to appoint counsel to represent them to minimise the possibility of this happening.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What may, however, warrant more attention is the concern raised by the Criminal Bar in the past, that they sometimes feel like they are battling a perception that criminal work plays second fiddle to civil and commercial matters and that they struggle to attract lawyers into their field.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Are there plans for officers in the Legal Service to be rotated into the PDO to allow greater exposure to the work that public defence entails?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: After all, Public Prosecutors are responsible for bringing cases against accused persons and thus represent the other side of the coin in the criminal justice system.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: To round up, I would like to touch on the important principle of justice being kept accessible and comprehensible.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is where public education is crucial in helping the public to understand the important role played by defence counsel, and by extension, Public Defenders.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: After all, defence lawyers are there to, amongst others, ensure that an accused person is innocent until proven guilty, understands the charges being brought against him and safeguards the due process of law while an accused person's case is being brought before the courts.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This means that they both have duties to the Court and also to the public.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Public Officers are expected to uphold values of integrity, service and excellence and are governed by a code of conduct.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Ensuring that the public are aware of these duties and codes which Public Defenders are bound by will be key in convincing the public about the necessity of the PDO.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The PDO must thus ensure that its conduct is exemplary, standing up to intense scrutiny and that it provides an accused person of a proper defence.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A strong PDO would only further aid in ensuring that the robust house of justice continues to endure.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We commend the Government for putting forward this Bill to improve the access to justice for the underprivileged in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are heartened that in the aftermath of the Parti Liyani case, the PAP Government has followed through on its promise during the Singapore's Justice System Motion, to seriously consider and implement a Public Defenders Office (PDO).

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are supportive of the general scope of offences that the PDO is intended to cover.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, we think that the Government can do more.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A scaling co-paying model could easily be implemented to ensure that applicants pay their fair share of the defence and yet at the same time, increase access to legal representation for underprivileged people.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will also increase the potential business for criminal lawyers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Increasing access to justice cannot be measured in dollars and cents.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Every person should have a chance to present his best case in court with legal representation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Deputy Speaker, I rise in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Progressive Singapore Party commends the Government for putting forward this Bill to improve access to justice for the underprivileged in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are heartened that in the aftermath of the Parti Liyani case, the PAP Government has followed through on its promise during the Singapore’s Justice System Motion to seriously consider and implement a Public Defender’s Office (PDO).

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are supportive of the general scope of offences that the PDO is intended to cover.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, I think that the Government can widen the income eligibility criteria for criminal legal aid.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Minister Shanmugam has proposed in his Ministerial Statement in April to peg the eligibility for criminal legal aid at a per capita gross monthly household income of $1,500.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are of the view that this amount should be raised to $2,200, which is in line with our recommendation for Singapore to adopt a minimum living wage of $2,200 for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government may argue that this would unnecessarily drive up costs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, we note that this Bill gives the Chief Public Defender the right to require applicants to co-pay for the legal cost.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A scaling co-payment model could easily be implemented to ensure that applicants pay their fair share of their defence and yet at the same time, increase access to legal representation for underprivileged people.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In English): To conclude, Sir, I support the Bill and propose that the eligibility criteria for criminal legal aid be pegged to a per capita gross monthly household income of $2,200.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Deputy Speaker, I fully support the establishment of the Public Defender’s Office.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These particular factors may include the applicant's medical condition and caregiving obligations, among others.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is important that the authorities retain a certain amount of flexibility, as each defendant and case is different.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some families may also run into temporary problems and are not able to get aid.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): Deputy Speaker, Sir, the setting up of the Public Defender’s Office (PDO) will ensure that accused persons who are vulnerable will have access to representation and defence in Court and build confidence in our justice system.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There will be a new system of contracts for the lawyers in the private sector to provide legal aid services.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The PDO should be responsible for the contracts coupled with a declaration form that the lawyers hold valid practising licence and have been in active legal practice in criminal law for a minimum of three years with supporting cases.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This specifically designed criteria should be created for an effective introduction of the system.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The likely benefits of such a device in place will ensure the following.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, provide good or better quality services from private practices at equal or lower costs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second, create a better alignment in the objectives of the PDO than would be possible with private sector lawyers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Third, provide management information on the supply of criminal defence services that would not otherwise be available to it through contracting.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Fourth, provide a test or a benchmark for the cost and quality of the criminal defence services by private practitioners under the contracts.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Fifth, provide independent, high quality and value-for-money criminal defence services to the public.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Sixth, provide the PDO with benchmarking information to improve, implement, initiate and introduce better performance of the contracting regime with private practice lawyers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Seventh, raise the level of understanding within MinLaw of all issues faced by criminal defence lawyers in the provision of high quality services to the public.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Eighth, recruit, train and develop people to provide high quality criminal defence services in accordance to the objectives of the PDO.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Ninth, share with private practice lawyers in terms of forms and systems which are developed within the PDO to assist in the overall improvements in the provision of criminal defence services.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the longer term, the best approach will prove to be a mixed system, combining both private and staff lawyers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will produce better value for money for the taxpayers because the two systems will in effect both complement and compete against one another.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The cost of the salaried service will provide a benchmark, which can be used to assess whether prices charged by private lawyers are reasonable.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Staff lawyers will also give flexibility to fill gaps in the system, for example, the participation of too few law firms.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The PDO has a role to play in benchmarking and further developing quality standards in criminal defence.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It will perform an integral part of the service development of the criminal justice system.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The PDO will develop and demonstrate more efficient ways of delivering criminal defence services.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We can envisage a wider role for the PDO as an essential guarantor of quality standards, minimum costs and people-centric satisfaction in a more managed market for such services.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Accused persons who are unable to afford lawyers to represent them face an indomitable inequality of arms against the Public Prosecution.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Helping impecunious persons gain access to good quality legal representation evens the field and ensures that robust criminal defence is the not the preserve of only the well-to-do and instead is available to everyone.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The Law Society Pro Bono Services' Criminal Legal Aid Scheme (CLAS) had, amongst other organisations and programmes, served this function.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It will fill a lacuna in our rule of law institutions and create a more fair and equitable society.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But public defending is a new concept to Singaporeans and given our reputation for robustly enforcing our laws and regulations and given the Government's previous position that the hon Member Murali Pillai had spoken on, it is novel and perhaps even discombobulating for the public that the Government will now be required by law to provide or to arrange for the defence of persons accused of certain offences.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In time, it will become an accepted part of our criminal legal system but how it is perceived and how it is approached will depend on the information and education provided to the public on this new setup and how the office carries out its statutory functions when it is set up.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, I have several points for the hon Senior Parliamentary Secretary's consideration.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: First, as there may not be sufficient understanding of the structure of the state as regards its legal components, it would be important to step up public education on how the public prosecutor is an independent organ of state and not part of MinLaw, which the PDO would be.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Often, laymen tend to lump all official bodies under the broad heading of the Government.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, the Public Prosecutor and MinLaw and the PDO as part of the Ministry are distinct and the public prosecutor is not part of the Government.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It may be otherwise confusing to the layman that the Government is funding both prosecution and defence and this was mentioned by earlier speakers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I note that clause 12(3) does provide that the Public Defender must not determine the benefit or detriment of a case based on the interests of the prosecution or of any other law enforcement agency.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Second, as the Public Defender will be providing a service to impecunious persons who may be elderly or who may not be highly educated, it is important that the process of making an application should be easy and accessible.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This would include having various modes of application, including online and in different languages, and assistance to make an application.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, to improve access, would the Senior Parliamentary Secretary consider providing a standard allocution for Police officers to recite to accused persons as regards having an option to avail of public defence when that person is being charged?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Further to this, I would also suggest that the period for considering an application should not be too lengthy while, of course, giving enough time for the PDO to carefully consider whether the application meets the criteria.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: An accused person would naturally have anxiety as to how they are going to deal with their case and many would be relying on legal aid to help them get through the criminal process.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: A timely response would ease their minds if they get the grant of aid.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: If they did not, it would allow them sufficient time to quickly pursue other options, including preparing to self-litigate.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: When a case is taken up, it is important to manage the expectations of persons receiving aid, in particular as to what are the prospects for their case as regards both verdict and sentence.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I am a little concerned that there may be backlash against the office by the accused person and their family members where a desired outcome in a particular case is not achieved.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As regards the performance of the Public Defenders, I note that in many jurisdictions that have such institutions, the common feedback is that Public Defenders have huge caseloads and are overworked to the point that they are not able to spend the necessary time and effort on each case.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This leads to less than optimal performance and quality of defence.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: So, it is not a small number of cases.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, we need to ensure that the PDO is adequately staffed, of course, with a prudent budget and that there is careful monitoring of each Public Defender's case load so that they take up a manageable number of cases.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: On a related note, we must ensure that the Public Defenders are also adequately compensated and have career progression prospects.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: While they should, of course, have passion in what they do, the PDO should not be a passion project, as it is in many other jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
