text: I would expect that because the Public Defenders would come under the Legal Service Officer scheme, their compensation would be competitive and that good lawyers will be attracted to join and stay in the office to build seniority and institutional knowledge.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This will help ensure a high standard of defence provided.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I am also gratified that the Bill provides for the involvement of lawyers in private practice via panels of lawyers who can be assigned to cases.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The private sector has carried the pro bono defence for many years and this spirit of public service to assist impecunious persons remains strong in the legal fraternity.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I would suggest that the panel of lawyers can be utilised in two ways: one, to assign cases to lawyers whose particular expertise would be useful in those cases; and two, as a release valve when the PDO's caseload gets too voluminous.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that there will also be avenues for Public Defenders and private lawyers to be able to work together on appropriate cases to leverage each other's knowledge and experience in defending the aid recipient.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In addition to what I have covered, I have the following clarifications on specific clauses.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This is relevant where a person had, for example, litigated in person in the first instance and then seeks help for an appeal after the verdict in the lower Court.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This would help to build complementarity between the PDO and other pro bono schemes.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In many cases of private prosecution, the prosecuting party appoints lawyers to pursue its or their case.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It provides access to justice that bolsters the rule of law.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding my suggestions and clarifications, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Globally, billions of people lack access to basic justice services and the most vulnerable are often women, children, people with disabilities and people from minority ethnic communities.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is thus important to address this justice gap.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While Singapore has a leading legal system and great access to justice already, we must continue to ensure that the most vulnerable segments of our society get the fair representation that they deserve in our criminal justice system – which is why this Bill is important.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I welcome and stand in support of this Bill and I would like to applaud MinLaw for this step towards greater access to justice.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Malay):   In October 2020, I asked whether the Government would consider providing direct legal aid to those with lesser financial means, who have been charged with criminal offences.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This was in light of concerns raised about access to justice and adequate legal representation for such persons, following the case of Parti Liyani.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This Bill allows for access to justice for criminal cases.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Previously criminal legal aid is administered by the Law Society alone.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Based on my previous experience as an assigned solicitor with the Legal Aid Bureau and CLAS, I welcome the mechanism for provisional grant of legal aid and mechanism for approval by the Public Defenders Office board.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I also welcome the scope of cooperation and sharing of caseload between PDO, that will be established, and CLAS, that is administered by the Law Society, as this will enable accused persons to have access to reasonable legal representation and expertise.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With the setting up of the Public Defender's Office, I hope that more accused can get access to fair and equal representation in Court notwithstanding their position, status or financial standing.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, providing criminal or civil legal aid requires funding and resources.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, there is also an economics argument to improve access to justice in society.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition, public investments in legal aid are also found to generate net savings in terms of avoided shelter or housing costs.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For one to qualify for PDO aid, one would have to pass the means and merits test.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I have a few clarifications in this regard.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Already, it is higher than the civil legal aid criteria of $950 dollars.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Specifically on PCHI and definition of household members, I would like to ask, if there will be discretion on the part of the Chief Public Defender (CPD), to grant criminal legal aid, if the accused person (AP) is no longer residing in the household, but the NRIC reflects the same address?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How about APs who can actually afford private lawyers because their children can pay, but their children are not living with the AP?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I quote hon Member Mr Lim Biow Chuan's concern that there is need to safeguard against abuse of process.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is important to clarify that passing the means and merits criteria does not automatically mean criminal legal aid will be granted.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: PDO, or CPD, shall still retain discretion whether to issue grant of aid or not.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, I welcome clause 12(1)(d), which retains such discretion and this will cover the exceptional cases and prevent the decisions of CPD from being challenged unmeritoriously.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To illustrate this point: in October 2021, a US couple sued the Colorado Public Defender's Office for refusing to represent them in a criminal case.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Both of them earned less than $3,000 a year, which automatically qualifies them for a Public Defender under the Colorado Supreme Court's guidelines.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In Singapore, this may not be challenged because of the proposed clause 12(1)(d).

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, what about a straightforward plead guilty case, where the AP would require legal assistance to formulate a mitigation plea, for instance, for appropriate sentencing?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I propose that for such cases, aid should be granted because firstly, it will save time and resources for both AGC and CPD, if issues on sentencing are appropriately addressed; and secondly, it will be just if the appropriate sentencing is meted out, if the necessary mitigating factors are highlighted.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Next, in respect of co-accused situations now, clause 14 prevents PDO from acting for more than one accused person.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is rightly so, to prevent conflict of interest.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, how will PDO ascertain which accused persons PDO will represent?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Is it the one with the best merits, the one with the lowest means, or the one that is first in time of application?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In instances where it is equal and the co-accused person is deserving of representation, I welcome Senior Parliamentary Secretary saying that PDO may assign the case to CLAS.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope it would be the same for the other co-accused persons as well.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would not the breaches under the Public Defenders Act be more egregious and, thus, should attract more hefty penalties as a deterrent?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Given that, firstly, it amounts to a perversion of criminal justice; secondly, it mainly involves matters of policy and public interest, as opposed to civil claims; and thirdly, it involves wastage of public resources.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Lastly, I would like to highlight the important role that PDO plays in portraying the image and integrity of Singapore's criminal justice system, and therefore, it is very important to look into the following aspects.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The first is the practice of plea bargaining, which is practised in Singapore and may generally occur once an accused is charged.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The outcome of any plea bargain depends on various factors, including public interest, timing of the guilty pleas and so on.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is important to note, that while a guilty plea saves public resources, a plea bargain is not a given right.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: US Supreme Court Justice Anthony Kennedy once wrote: "Horse trading   determines who goes to jail and for how long.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is not some adjunct to the criminal justice system; it is the criminal justice system." The situation in US is possibly due to a disparity in funding of the two sides of the criminal justice system.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There was also lack of training and support for overworked Public Defenders and a lack of reform to the bail system which holds people in jail simply because they lack the funds to secure their own release.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In Singapore, with the establishment of PDO, it is important to ensure that our system does not devolve into a similar scenario like that in foreign countries.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I would propose for safeguards to be put in place to ensure that any plea bargain entered will be in the best interest of an AP and perhaps, these cases may have an avenue for review by an independent body with MinLaw and LawSoc's involvement.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I echo hon Member Mr Murali Pillai's suggestions for publication of KPIs.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Next, on avenue of redress, if complaints are raised about PDO officers, to which body would these complaints be referred?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For private or CLAS practitioners, they are governed under the professional conduct rules and referred to the Law Society.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My next point is on building up the capability of PDO officers.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is imperative that we attract and retain talent in PDO, to ensure that there are PDO officers with the appropriate trial experience.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I propose a secondment of AGC officers to PDO and for active recruitment from the criminal bar.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We need to dispel the myth that Public Defenders are not going to give a fair representation of any accused.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In fact, the converse may be true, studies show that Public Defenders perform better than the appointed counsel, that is, those who are counsel in private practice and paid by the system.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There were two factors that interviewees cited as important differences between public defenders and appointed counsel: firstly, Public Defenders use of integrated teams, which means greater access to non-legal professionals who may help in the defence; and, secondly, the larger amount of case preparation by Public Defenders.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What this means is that a robust training will create more opportunities for our PDO officers.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In terms of specialisations, perhaps there could be a setting up of dedicated teams within PDO, like that in AGC, arranged according to the types of offences, so that PDO officers can build up deep capability and skillsets, and secondly, a platform for the cross-training and sharing of ideas between prosecutors, PDO and the criminal bar.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have clarifications to raise in respect of three areas.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first area of clarification is on the scope of offences.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Ministry has announced that it is considering how best to define cases dealt with by the PDO and CLAS.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To prevent potential confusion, can Senior Parliamentary Secretary provide an update on how the cases will be scoped?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, under subsection 8(2), the grant of aid will not be granted to an offence excluded or belonging to an excluded class, as specified in the Schedule of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Ministry has explained that this Bill will exclude regulatory offences, minor departmental and Statutory Board charges.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, regulatory charges can carry potential jail terms.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Senior Parliamentary Secretary share why such offences are excluded from the grant of aid when the potential jail terms are no less than what is provided for other offences covered by the PDO, including those under the Penal Code.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second area of clarification is on the appointment and discharge of a solicitor.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, under subsection 8(8), a grant of aid may be extended to proceedings involving an excluded offence, if the applicant faces charges for two or more offences and one or more of which is an excluded offence, or if the appeal or application arises from the proceedings.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In criminal proceedings, it is common for charges to be withdrawn, taken into consideration, or replaced with alternative charges.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Senior Parliamentary Secretary share how a grant of aid may be affected in a situation where the prosecution exercises its discretion to withdraw, take into consideration, or replace charges such that the prosecution will only proceed on excluded offences?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Would this be ground for the withdrawal of a grant of aid?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If so, how will the PDO ensure that the defence of the applicant is not prejudiced by any withdrawal of aid?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, section 18 provides that criminal defence aid cannot be discontinued without the permission of the Chief Public Defender.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This means that even if an aided person no longer wishes to instruct a Public Defender, the accused person cannot discharge their solicitor without permission.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Practically speaking, it will be extremely difficult for a Public Defender to take instructions from an aided accused person who no longer wishes to be represented by the Public Defender.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: With any other solicitor-client relationship, a litigant is entitled to discharge their solicitor.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Senior Parliamentary Secretary clarify the rationale for requiring the permission of the Chief Public Defender before an aided accused person can discharge a solicitor assigned to act for them?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What are the situations where the Chief Public Defender may decline the accused person's request to discharge the Public Defender?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Third, under section 17, the Chief Public Defender may require an aided accused person to make contributions to a matter where a grant of aid has been provided.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In a situation where the aided accused person is unable to meet the contributions, can Senior Parliamentary Secretary share if this is ground for discontinuation of grant of aid?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If so, how will the PDO ensure that the defence of the applicant is not prejudiced by the withdrawal of aid?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My final area of clarification is on the relationship between AGC and PDO that many Members have raised.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The PDO will be a department under MinLaw.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that AGC is separate from MinLaw.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, AGC's functions include acting as the Government's lawyer and advising Ministries.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There may still be some potential areas of conflict given the proximity of MinLaw and the AGC.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Senior Parliamentary Secretary share what mechanisms are in place to address the potential areas of conflict and to ensure that the decision making and operations of the PDO are independent of AGC?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Notwithstanding these clarifications, Sir, I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In 1985, the late Mr Harry Elias, Senior Counsel, along with several counsel members of the Law Society, spearheaded the setting up of the Law Society's Criminal Legal Aid Scheme, in short, CLAS, to help the less fortunate to obtain free criminal legal representation.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Since then, the Law Society's mission to grant better access to justice and ensure criminal legal aid for needy and deserving accused facing a criminal charge never wavered.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It must be remembered that every accused person is innocent unless proven guilty and he or she is entitled to seek legal representation to defend himself or herself.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And as recounted by my Parliamentary colleague, Mr Murali Pillai, earlier in his speech, I am glad that the Government has also stepped in over the years to support this meaningful endeavour.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I envision that the end result of institutionalising public defence in our criminal justice system to include the following.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: First, enabling more vulnerable applicants to apply and receive criminal legal criminal legal aid swiftly.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And thirdly, to cultivate an ecosystem devoted recruiting, retaining and motivating more people to pursue criminal defence as a profession.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This flexibility is needed as the situation that requires it can vary in detail.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: An example would be an accused person charged under the Common Gaming House Act.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They could either be intellectually disabled or induced to be a lookout for a common gaming house or a gullible teenager who has been influenced by peer pressure to be a bookie.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In both scenarios, if the family members of the accused do not have the financial means to assist to seek legal representation for them, these situations will be undesirable unless they were granted aid due to such special circumstances.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: On the same point as what Mr Lim Biow Chuan has raised earlier in his speech, we have often heard of cases where applicants who have already been in remand for a period of time are still waiting for their request for legal representation to be processed.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To prevent situations where the remanded period ends up being longer than what a Court might eventually sentence the accused for, I think it is important that PDO ensures that the application process and the time taken to review the application is as straightforward and as swift as possible to reduce the possibility of such occurrences.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With both PDO and CLAS operating as independent entities, would an applicant be required to make duplicated requests for aid?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I hope that a single centralised system can be implemented.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I understand that PDO is looking to bolster their manpower by bringing in a wave of fresh graduates, young lawyers, mid-career hires and Legal Service Officers.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But apart from meeting the required numbers, I firmly believe that there is a real need to ensure the quality of the service to be provided.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To ensure consistency in terms of the quality of the legal representation provided by each of the Public Defenders, be its in-house Public Defenders or those engaged under the panel of qualified lawyers, the PDO may wish to consider collaborating with the Law Society of Singapore's Advocacy Committee, the Criminal Practice Committee and the CLAS Committee, in working out a series of training sessions to sharpen the skills of the lawyers in areas such as the advocacy and criminal procedures.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In a Mass Call Address 2021, the hon Chief Justice Sundaresh Menon have shared that and I quote, "The pro bono spirit is among the very best tradition of our Bar.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Few things are more precious than the opportunity to help someone who has been shut out from the access to justice." As a lawyer, we are trained to be the person who unlocks that door.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The Chief Justice strongly encouraged the newly minted lawyers to actively seek opportunities for involvement in pro bono work and CLAS was cited as an excellently meaningful avenue for pro bono service.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am glad that, moving forward, the PDO will also be another available option for one to contribute accordingly, However, the reality of our legal profession is that criminal defence is not widely regarded as lucrative work and that those who pursue it as a career are often driven by passion and a conviction to help others.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As a result, many young lawyers may not be exposed to doing criminal defence work unless he or she are in firms which support pro bono initiatives or do criminal defence work on a frequent basis.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But just as what the hon Chief Justice has shared in the Mass Call Address, young lawyers should, which I quote, "Learn to lean on the community, look for role models and mentors to whom you can turn for guidance and inspirations." In this regard, I hope that PDO would be opened to having young lawyers with little experience to volunteer and be included in its panel of solicitors for cases in their capacity as a junior assistant counsel.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is similar to what is currently practised under the Legal Assistance Scheme for Capital Offences, in short, LASCO, which allows relatively inexperienced lawyers to observe proceedings and provide some support for the lead counsel, allowing them to be exposed to much needed experience in criminal legal matters.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As a further suggestion, we can perhaps also consider giving this junior assistant counsel Continuing Professional Development (CPD) points instead of offering honorariums.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, I support this Bill to establish the Public Defenders’ Office (PDO).

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The PDO will provide greater legal assistance to the underprivileged group when they are unfortunately embroiled in criminal proceedings.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Ultimately, all the cost will be borne by taxpayers.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: (In English): Notwithstanding the above clarifications and suggestions, I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A key aspect of the rule of law is access to justice, not just for some, but for all Singaporeans, regardless of their means.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I would first like to commend the Government's readiness to regularly relook this position as our society matures and to shift its policy accordingly.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Where the Government has previously taken a position that criminal legal aid should not be publicly funded, today, we are debating a Bill that would render assistance to Singapore residents if they are charged with certain criminal offences.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, we can build a fairer society based on justice and equality.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Speaking as someone who is not legally trained, I would like to seek some clarifications on the Bill and the proposed Public Defender's Office (PDO).

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First, from the practical perspective of a person who may use and benefit from the PDO's services and second, on the operational and structural aspects of the PDO.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In Malay):   The law cannot just be a rich man’s game or for the wealthy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Today, there are various options for people to get free legal advice or answers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: You can book appointments with legal clinics at the CDCs and CCs to talk to a volunteer lawyer.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The iLAB chatbot on the MinLaw's website also provides legal information on issues related to family and divorce issues.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On the other hand, there are lesser schemes for people to get legal representation in Court.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is especially so bearing in mind the current state of high inflation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, if there are multiple co-accused qualifying for PDO assistance, how would the PDO choose which case to take up?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One other issue is regarding centralising legal aid in general.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With the creation of the PDO, is there an intention to centralise legal aid into a one-stop shop?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Ordinary Singaporeans may not know which specific agency to approach for their matters.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, the PDO, the Legal Assistance Scheme for Capital Offences (LASCO) and the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme (CLAS) will provide legal representation for different types of criminal offences.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Legal Aid Bureau (LAB) may provide legal representation for certain civil proceedings.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: All these must also be distinguished from the agencies that provide free legal advice but not representation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I understand that clause 12(5) of the Bill already empowers the Chief Public Defender to refer an application to another suitable body or organisation providing pro bono legal services.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Going one step further to provide a one-stop shop to direct Singaporeans to the legal aid they need – and which they qualify for – all these will definitely be helpful.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In English): There are some offences that the PDO will not cover and it looks like quite a long list.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some of the excluded offences appear to be offences that ordinary Singaporeans would likely get into trouble for and require legal aid for.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Such as offences under the Road Traffic Act or regulatory offences under the purview of certain Statutory Boards.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Clause 12(8) of the Bill also helpfully clarifies that a person may still obtain legal representation from the PDO even if he is charged with multiple offences and if one or more of them is an excluded offence.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, will such an applicant be treated differently?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will he be required to co-pay a pro-rata share of the legal expenses corresponding to the excluded offences?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Next, on clause 17 of the Bill which allows the Chief Public Defender to require a legal aid applicant to co-fund his legal defence, would that be the norm or the exception?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In principle, some degree of balancing would be required to prevent abuse of the legal aid that is provided.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Talking to some lawyers, I have heard stories of legal aid applicants who are less than cooperative with the volunteer lawyers who take up their defence pro bono, especially when the applicants need not fork out a single cent for their defence.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, a default co-funding arrangement may not entirely be a bad thing.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It will of course be necessary to calibrate the amount of co-funding on a case-by-case basis considering the applicant's financial and other circumstances.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In terms of timing, at which point in time will the applicant be informed of the contributions that he will have to make?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Save for special circumstances, any financial burden should be fully disclosed to the applicant at the outset of the legal aid application.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Any uncertainty would detract from the objective of allaying our vulnerable residents' concern over accumulating legal fees; which is quite important.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope Senior Parliamentary Secretary can help answer that question later on.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is also an overlap between the space that the PDO will occupy and the space occupied by volunteer lawyers who take up criminal defence cases pro bono.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Have there been any studies on whether there are particular types of criminal defence cases that private practitioners are more willing, or less willing, to take up pro bono?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: From an efficiency standpoint, PDO should complement the existing pro bono efforts of our lawyers and multiply the potential reach of criminal legal aid in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As PDO is also aimed at developing expertise, building up institutional knowledge and access to expert witnesses, medical and forensic analysts and so on, will private lawyers volunteering under CLAS be allowed to tap on PDO's precedents and knowledge?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This would reassure the public that there would be minimal difference in outcomes to prefer the criminal legal aid provided by PDO, or that provided by volunteer lawyers through schemes like CLAS.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I ask this primarily because I am concerned that the Chief Public Defender's decisions to grant or not grant aid may potentially be politicised especially where specific individuals or offences are involved.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Such concerns would have been substantially reduced if PDO and the Chief Public Defender had been given an independent role under the Singapore Constitution.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As the famous saying goes, "Justice must not only be done, but must also be seen to be done".

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I believe that the PDO will help to reduce the inequality in our criminal justice system, by providing legal representation to the vulnerable and low-income citizens and PRs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Notwithstanding, I have several clarifications on the PDO Bill.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, there needs to be clearer delineation of the various legal help channels available to low-income groups who face criminal proceedings.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: One is the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme (CLAS).

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There may be an overlap in matters covered by both CLAS and the PDO.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: One way to ensure efficient resource allocation is to create a clearer distinction between the nature and the types of cases that the PDO and CLAS should respectively take on.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The PDO hires full-time lawyers and pays them for their work.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: On the other hand, lawyers under CLAS volunteer their services and expertise.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, I believe it would be fairer for the PDO to take up more complex cases.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They should also take up the bulk of the cases.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The PDO, with more resources at its disposal, may be better positioned to handle the greater workload.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is compared to pro bono lawyers who often have to manage other paid work concurrently.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In fact, how would the interplay between CLAS and PDO evolve the legal aid landscape in the future, for instance, for offences that are covered by CLAS and not PDO, and vice versa.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, what about offences that are not covered by CLAS or PDO?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will there be regular reviews as to what offences should be included or excluded for aid granted under CLAS or PDO?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In this regard, who should inform the accused of the aid available?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is particularly important since the person would usually be in a very stressful situation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Would it be possible to use the Public Defenders Bill to also provide for such a support structure?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: On a related note, with the establishment of the PDO, it is imperative to communicate the different avenues of legal help to the public in clear and simple terms.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To many, the legal system is not something that crosses the mind of one on a regular basis.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How does the Government intend to do this, so that the average Joe can understand and navigate the various means for free or subsidised legal support?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Community legal clinic volunteers should also be advised, so that they are able to dispense timely and up-to-date information.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Ultimately, both initiatives, in addition to the functions of the Legal Aid Bureau, need to be clearly positioned, to avoid potential confusion by the public.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The idea of broadening access to justice through the setting up of the PDO should not be narrowly construed.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: No one, regardless of the alleged offence committed, should be less deserving of access to legal representation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Related to the above, should regulatory offences be included?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Members Mr Louis Ng and Mr Saktiandi also raised this point.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For instance, should serious traffic offences be covered under the PDO?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are the accused eligible for legal assistance or criminal legal aid for serious traffic offences that carry potential jail terms?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Serious traffic offences are often complex in nature.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I refer to accidents where multiple parties or even the victim could be partially responsible.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The high stakes make it even more critical that the accused parties have the necessary resources to legal aid.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I have met residents at my Meet-the-People session (MPS), who were involved in serious traffic offences and needed help.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, traffic offences which carry the risk of custodial sentences, do not appear to be covered under CLAS.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I pause here to note that whilst the assumption is that most drivers have adequate means, we must not forget that several drivers do not own the vehicles that they are operating.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some may be private hire or taxi drivers too.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, ensuring cost efficiency is a must.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is especially so in the current economic climate.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Now, the intention is to have the PDO publicly funded.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will the Government ensure that the costs do not spiral?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There are calls for the Government to cover more people with higher income under the PDO Scheme.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While it is good to ask, we should also be mindful of how it is going to be paid for by the Government and how the public taxpayers' money is spent.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Minister had previously cited cases of abuse in his Statement.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In some of these cases, the accused persons may meet the means and merits eligibility criteria but could be morally undeserving of aid.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: One example was a war criminal in Australia, who incurred closed to $1 million in costs to defend him.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It does not necessarily take a crime of international impact to be widely considered morally reprehensible among citizens.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: One example is the case of violent crimes against children, like sexual assault or severe abuse.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Moreover, what safeguards are there to prevent people from misusing the PDO to make all sorts of appeals against the legal process?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Having safeguards on keeping costs down would also go some ways in preventing abuse of the legal process.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: An example of such an application can be seen from the recent appeal of an appellant, against her sentence of 30 years imprisonment for, amongst others, the killing of her maid.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Therein, the Court of Appeal found the factors which were raised in the appeal to be wholly without merit.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fourth, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, we need to ensure adequate manpower for the PDO, which will consist of an entirely new department.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Private law firms continue to report a talent crunch.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Ministry share statistics on how many practising criminal lawyers are there currently in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How can we recruit adequate talents to fill the new roles?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And how do we attract more criminal lawyers, without adversely affecting the rest of the criminal law landscape in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fifth, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, we must strike a balance with protecting the victims' legal rights.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What about circumstances where victims that wish to separately seek personal redress and private prosecution is needed?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For example, if the injury is not particularly serious, but these victims may want to seek a vindication of their rights.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If they are unable to afford lawyers and are too emotionally distressed and tied up to navigate the legal process with minimal support, who can they turn to for help?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are there cases where victims feel pressured to drop charges, or to settle for the first offer of compensation, due to the lack of funds?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Who can victims turn to in such situations?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This should be regardless of their financial circumstances.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I have met some of these vulnerable residents at my MPS.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: He works in the F&B sector and was charged with committing a criminal offence while he was drunk.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: He came to see me at the MPS as his last resort.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While he could be eligible for certain pro bono legal services, he was unsure of where to seek help.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Community Legal Clinics could take weeks to see an applicant and only for 20 minutes each time.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Mr C was anxious that he would not have fair access to justice, taking into consideration that the nature of his offence was rather complex.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The PDO will help to provide assurance to residents like Mr C.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We would be a dead society if we do not make every effort to lift people up from the bottom.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need to have a criminal justice system where dedicated officers have their eyes, ears and hearts open to the difficulties underprivileged people face and to make the Courts see that pain and respond.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is an exalted mission, a mission of maximum importance by releasing underprivileged people from their bondage of powerlessness.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As part of the larger system, the PDO will narrow the gap between the rich and the poor and more importantly, it keeps the promise of justice and equality alive for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai suggested that this Bill arises from the Motion concerning Ms Parti Liyani's case.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: He might recall that the Minister for Law had specifically stated that the Ministry had started reviewing our criminal legal model and how we provide aid, in 2018 and 2019.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: He repeated this point during his Ministerial Statement in April this year.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Members have raised questions and suggestions on the structure and management of the Public Defender’s Office (PDO), specific provisions in the Public Defenders Bill and the provision of aid by both PDO and the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme (CLAS).

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I will address each bucket of issues in turn.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat, Mr Louis Ng, Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim and Mr Lim Biow Chuan asked about the independence of the PDO and if there would be any conflict of interest between the PDO and the Attorney-General’s Chambers (AGC).

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: First, this ensures that the Government has oversight over the PDO.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The structure we have adopted for the PDO follows a study of various common law jurisdictions, such as the UK, Australia, New Zealand and Hong Kong.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The offices in these jurisdictions are accountable to the Executive arm but retain independence in day-to-day operations.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This accountability is necessary to ensure better governance and fiscal control.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Second, this structure ensures independence from the Prosecution, which is under AGC.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Officers in the PDO, or PD Officers, will be employed directly by MinLaw and are placed on a different scheme from the officers in AGC.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: They will report to the Permanent Secretary and Minister for Law.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This ensures a clear separation of powers and responsibilities from the Prosecution.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We want talent flows from AGC, but we want to be careful to maintain independence.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We are working out how this can be done and whether it should be secondment or some other mechanism.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This will provide opportunities for knowledge sharing, job exposure and career development for the officers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The PDO will start modestly and scale up over time.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We will review the PDO at an appropriate juncture and assess the PDO’s needs in the medium and long term, based on the trends from its initial years of operation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: On cost controls, I spoke earlier about the means and merits tests that function as key checkpoints.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We want to ensure that aid only goes to those who deserve it.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We will work with other agencies to ensure that our budget is well-managed.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Murali Pillai, Mr Yip Hon Weng, Ms Hany Soh, Mr Raj Joshua Thomas and Ms He Ting Ru asked about the recruitment and remuneration of PD Officers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We are in the process of recruiting suitable candidates via a robust selection process.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We are looking for individuals with both the heart and necessary legal qualifications and skills.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I am heartened to say that there has been a very good response from both fresh graduates and mid-career lawyers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We are also reviewing our staff remuneration package and career development opportunities to ensure that the PDO is competitive enough to attract and retain talent.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We will monitor the caseload of the PDO to see that there is adequate staffing and capacity.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I would also like to assure Mr Yip Hon Weng and Ms He Ting Ru that the PDO is not here to compete with the Criminal Bar.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We intend for the PDO to be an important stakeholder in the criminal justice system and play its part to develop a competent and reputable Bar.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The PDO also provides an additional avenue for lawyers to engage in community work and serve vulnerable communities.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We will consider Ms Hany Soh’s suggestions on working with the Law Society to organise trainings for our officers and for young lawyers in private practice to have the opportunity to volunteer for cases with the PDO.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Murali Pillai, Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim and Mr Raj Joshua Thomas asked how we could manage the quality of our PD Officers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Our aim is that the pool of PD Officers will comprise a healthy mix of experienced criminal lawyers, young lawyers and fresh graduates.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The officers will, obviously, have to act in the best interests of the aided accused person during plea bargaining, an area of concern highlighted by Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim asked how complaints against PD Officers would be handled.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: As mentioned in my opening speech, PD Officers are subject to the same disciplinary framework as Judicial and Legal Service Officers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: As public officers, PD Officers are also subject to internal disciplinary proceedings if they misconduct themselves.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked for data on accused persons who have legal representation and how that relates to the number of acquittals when they claim trial.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: However, it may not be fair or accurate to measure success in terms of acquittal and to measure that against legal representation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: As Mr Murali Pillai pointed out, there are many factors that affect the outcome of a case – legal representation is one of many.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I assure Mr Murali Pillai that our focus is on ensuring that those who need and are deserving of help, get help.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked how many more people will receive legal representation when the PDO is established, compared to the number represented by CLAS.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat also asked about the provision of criminal defence aid for the bottom 35% of households by income.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: As I mentioned earlier, we raised our income coverage to the 35th percentile because our analysis showed that individuals up to this income threshold would find it challenging to pay for their legal costs, even for a plead guilty case.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We have to balance providing sustainable aid, while exercising prudence in the use of public funds.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Ms He Ting Ru asked about the provision of aid to non-Singaporeans and Permanent Residents.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Non-SCPRs can look at other avenues for legal aid.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng was concerned that the public might find it repugnant if tax dollars go towards supporting accused persons who are viewed as morally reprehensible.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: As the Minister for Law had raised in his Ministerial Statement in April, public outrage alone cannot be the basis upon which criminal defence aid should or should not be provided.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Rather, these assessments will be made based on the legal merits of the applicant's case.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Murali Pillai suggested that the PDO and the Prosecution can explore the joint appointment of experts that will bind both sides.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This is not the current practice for criminal cases.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Currently, the Prosecution, generally, asks for the accused person to undergo a forensic psychiatric assessment only after the accused person is charged in Court.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Likewise, the PDO will have the avenue for doing so even after the accused person is charged in Court.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: As for the early involvement of the PDO in certain cases, the Bill is only intended to cover criminal defence aid to accused persons who have been charged in Court and not those under investigations.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Not all investigations result in criminal charges in Court.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It is not fiscally prudent to extend aid to accused persons who are still under investigations.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh and Mr Raj Joshua Thomas suggested how we could manage the lawyers we outsource cases to.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked what conditions need to be satisfied before the PDO will outsource cases to lawyers in private practice.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The selection process to appoint solicitors onto the panel for outsourced cases will be stringent.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Only solicitors who are sufficiently skilled and with a good track record in handling criminal cases will be appointed.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: On Mr Lim Biow Chuan’s question about how we will pay these lawyers, these are operational matters which we are still working out.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Murali Pillai proposed to amend the definition of “court” in clause 2 of the Bill to limit to Courts constituted under the Supreme Court of Judicature Act 1969 or the State Courts Act 1970.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I should, first, highlight that the Bill is intended to include criminal proceedings tried in a Family Court or a Youth Court.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: A Family Court and a Youth Court are not constituted under the State Courts Act 1970 or the Supreme Court of Judicature Act 1969.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Murali Pillai’s proposed amendment, therefore, excludes the Family Court and Youth Court, which can exercise criminal jurisdiction.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The definition in the Bill is clear and our position is that an amendment is not needed.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The scope of criminal defence aid is determined by the scope of proceedings in clauses 8(1) and 12(8), which have been carved out to only cover criminal proceedings.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The definition of "court” cannot be looked at in vacuum.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Under the Criminal Procedure Code, criminal proceedings are heard by the Court of Appeal, the General Division of the High Court, a Family Court, a Youth Court, a District Court or a Magistrate’s Court, which exercises criminal jurisdiction.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The intent is to only provide criminal defence aid to criminal proceedings before these Courts.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The term “criminal proceedings” does not contemplate other types of proceedings, such as those before the Subordinate Military Courts, the Military Court of Appeal or the Industrial Arbitration Courts.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Moreover, proceedings before Military Courts are only against persons subject to military law.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In light of the clarification above, I hope that Mr Murali Pillai will withdraw his Notice of Amendment.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng, Mr Saktiandi Supaat, Mr Louis Ng, Mr Lim Biow Chuan and Ms Hany Soh asked about the exclusion of offences under various legislation listed in the Schedule.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In other words, if an accused person is charged in Court after being arrested or is issued an arrest warrant, their offences under these specified legislation are included.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: These offences tend to be more serious in nature.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The same applies to accused persons who have been arrested and charged for more serious traffic offences under the Road Traffic Act, which is one of the specified Acts.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Accused persons can apply for criminal defence aid for these offences.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: On Mr Yip Hon Weng’s concern that not all drivers are well-off, they can qualify for aid as long as they pass our means and merits tests, so long as the offence is not an excluded one.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Our decision not to provide aid for regulatory or minor offences is in line with many other jurisdictions, where certain offences which are less serious are also excluded.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: For example, in Ontario, Canada, aid is restricted to offences that are indictable or which carry a risk of incarceration.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We have to strike a balance between providing aid for all offences and ensuring that costs are sustainable.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We also recognise that in a single set of proceedings, an accused person may face multiple charges, some of which are excluded offences.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: If granted aid, they will not be treated any differently.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The amount of contributions required will be based on the applicant's means rather than the type of offences which he or she is charged with.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The PDO will see through the matter until the criminal proceedings have concluded, even if the non-excluded proceedings are withdrawn or replaced mid-way, leaving only excluded proceedings.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Where charges are taken into consideration, these remain part of the criminal proceedings.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: On Ms Hany Soh's request for discretion to provide aid for offences under the 10 Acts specified in paragraph 1(1)(d) of the Schedule, we have explained the reason for their exclusion.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: These are Acts whose primary purpose is to deter certain behaviours which are morally depraved or bring about significant negative externalities to society.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Nonetheless, we will monitor and periodically review the list of excluded offences after the PDO has commenced operations.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: If we find excluded offences that are assessed to be deserving of aid, we can subsequently amend the list of excluded offences.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked about the provision of aid for Legal Assistance Scheme for Capital Offences (LASCO) matters.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: MinLaw remains open to the possibility of the PDO covering capital offences at a later stage.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim, Mr Lim Biow Chuan and Mr Leong Mun Wai asked about the specifics of our means and merits test criteria.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng also asked about the safeguards to prevent the use of the PDO's resources for frivolous appeals.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Our means test criteria is largely aligned with that of civil legal aid and other social support schemes where we look at the per capita household income (PCHI).

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai suggested increasing the PCHI to S$2,200.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: As Ms Hany Soh said, in a family of four, that would be S$6,000.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We have tried to be prudent in spending taxpayers' monies.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The House knows that expenditures are increasing and there is some resistance to how we raise the monies needed.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It depends on the available funds as well.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We are mindful that there may be applicants who have extenuating or special circumstances such as those listed by Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I assure Mr Lim Biow Chuan that we have robust measures in place to check that an applicant is not hiding his or her income and assets.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It will be an offence for an applicant to provide false or misleading statements to obtain aid.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: As for our merits test criteria, I assure Mr Yip Hon Weng that the Chief PD will assess the merits of any application before deciding if aid should be granted to the applicant.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Even if an applicant satisfies the means and merits criteria, the Chief PD can decide whether to grant aid depending on whether it is appropriate to do so.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The Chief PD will consider factors such as those in clause 12(2) of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: These include whether the applicant is likely to lose his or her livelihood if any matter in the proceedings is decided against him or her, whether any benefit may accrue to the applicant if criminal defence aid is granted and our resource constraints.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This discretion allows aid to be given to those who need it most.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: To circle back to Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim's question, aid can certainly be granted to an applicant who intends to plead guilty, for the purposes of formulating a mitigation plea for sentencing, so long as the requirements to the means and merits are satisfied.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas asked about the provision of aid for criminal appeals and criminal applications.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Aid can be provided to such applicants, even if it was not provided at first instance.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Where an applicant is unsuccessful in his application, the referral mechanism under clause 12(5) will not be applicable.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The applicant can seek aid from organisations providing pro bono legal services such as the Law Society Pro Bono Services' Ad Hoc Pro Bono Assessment Scheme.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Next, Mr Lim Biow Chuan, Ms Hany Soh and Mr Raj Joshua Thomas queried the speed at which the merits and means tests are conducted.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: For instance, because the accused has been in remand for some time or by virtue of the accused person's age.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We will work with the Singapore Prisons Service and the Courts to ensure that these urgent cases are handled expeditiously.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: On Ms Sylvia Lim's question regarding the deliberation of non-prescribed offences by the board, the presence of the board allows for greater deliberation of offences which carry a more serious consequence on the applicant.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Regarding Ms He Ting Ru's suggestion on an appeals mechanism, none is provided.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: After we get some experience with the PDO, we will consider whether such an appeals mechanism will be useful.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked if contributions will be a norm and when an applicant will be informed of the contributions required.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Louis Ng asked if an applicant's aid will be discontinued if he or she is unable to make the contribution.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: As I mentioned earlier, the amount of contributions is decided based on the means of the applicant.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Any contribution required will be made known to the applicant before aid is granted.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: If an aided person is unable to pay, we will take into account any extenuating circumstances and will work with him or her to meet the contribution.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan and Mr Raj Joshua Thomas asked about the provision of criminal defence aid to multiple co-accused persons.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim also asked how the PDO would choose which cases to take up if there are multiple co-accused persons.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This would be the case whether the co-accused person decides to plead guilty or claim trial.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: For example, an accused person in remand may require more urgent representation, which can be provided by the PDO.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked about how the PDO will deal with accused persons with mental illnesses.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: While an accused may have mental illnesses, he may not lack cognitive abilities and can give instructions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: If he lacks mental capacity, there are provisions in the Mental Capacity Act for an application to Court to be made for a deputy to make decisions on the person's behalf.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: If the accused person cannot give proper instructions to his or her solicitor or PD officer because of a mental condition, the Court can call for a psychiatric assessment to determine whether the person is of unsound mind and incapable of making a defence.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: There are provisions under our law for Court proceedings to be held off if an accused person is found to be of unsound mind.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan asked about the extent that clause 4(5) may affect legal professional privilege and confidentiality applicable to communications between an assigned solicitor and an aided accused person.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Such information may be necessary to enable the Chief PD to make a fully considered decision.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We recognise and respect the confidentiality that exists within a client-and-solicitor relationship but such confidentiality is subject to exceptions even within the Legal Profession (Professional Conduct) Rules and includes situations where the disclosure is permitted or required by law.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: On Ms Sylvia Lim's question regarding a witness who lies to a Public Defender and whether he or she will be committing an offence, not all untruths will be covered.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: There will be instances where the individual lies about the means of the aided accused person in relation to the grant of aid.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In such instances, the conduct will be covered.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Louis Ng, Mr Murali Pillai, Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim and Mr Lim Biow Chuan asked about processes relating to the termination of criminal defence aid.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Louis Ng and Mr Lim Biow Chuan asked about the discharge of an assigned solicitor.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Clause 18 governs the relationship between an aided accused person and an assigned solicitor.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It does not cover the representation of an aided accused person by PD officers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Clause 18 is intended to address a situation where, for example, an aided accused person repeatedly seeks to change the assigned solicitor to delay the criminal proceedings.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The criminal defence aid scheme should not be used for such abuses of process.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: When deciding whether to grant permission for the aided accused person to discharge an assigned solicitor or for an assigned solicitor to discontinue the provision of criminal defence aid, the Chief PD will consider all relevant factors, including any reasons provided by the aided accused person and the assigned solicitor.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked about the cancellation of aid.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We expect that the factors under Regulation 8 of the Legal Aid and Advice Regulations would generally apply here.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: For example, a grant of aid may be cancelled if the applicant provides false information in the application for criminal defence aid.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Where a grant of aid is cancelled, the PDO will work with the aided accused person and/or his or her subsequent solicitors to minimise any disruption to the criminal proceedings and ensure the proper administration of justice.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: As for Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim's question on the offence for making a false or misleading statement, this is equally egregious whether someone is applying for criminal defence aid or civil legal aid.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Both are criminal offences and are a waste of public resources.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: On Mr Lim Biow Chuan's query regarding a solicitor who has been excluded from the panel of solicitors, the Bill does not cover and the PDO will not interfere with the relationship between solicitors and accused persons who are both outside of the criminal defence aid scheme.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: As for whether such a solicitor can continue with a frivolous Court application, there are existing provisions within the Criminal Procedure Code (CPC) which will address such conduct.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng expressed concern that some victims may wish to seek personal redress through private actions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas also asked about private prosecutions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Thorough investigations are conducted by our Police and the AGC considers criminal complaints seriously before determining if charges should be brought against accused persons.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Where a criminal charge is brought and the accused person is found guilty, the Court may also make an order for compensation to the victim, where appropriate.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This process does not require the victim to engage his or her own legal representation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: If a victim wishes to take up private prosecution against an alleged perpetrator, the victim can file a Magistrate's complaint.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The Courts have put in place mediation facilities to assist such private disputes, which are intentionally simplified so that there is no real need for legal representation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Hence, criminal defence aid is not provided for private prosecutions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: If the victim wishes to take up a private civil suit and cannot afford a lawyer, he or she may apply for civil legal aid with the Legal Aid Bureau.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Ultimately, we want to provide aid to those who need aid, but in a sustainable manner.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng, Mr Louis Ng, Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Ms Sylvia Lim noted that the PDO would overlap with CLAS and asked what cases would be handled by each outfit.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat, Mr Yip Hon Weng and Ms Hany Soh also proposed centralising all legal aid.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: CLAS remains an important partner and player in the criminal justice system.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We will continue to work with CLAS to provide criminal defence aid.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This will ensure a sustainable and effective legal aid system.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The assignment of cases to PDO or CLAS will be done at the backend.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Broadly, there is a two-step process for deciding which cases go to PDO or CLAS.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: First, the case would be assessed for urgency.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This ensures that legal representation is provided as early as possible.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Second, the remaining cases will be shared between PDO and CLAS.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The actual number of cases taken on by PDO or CLAS would depend on factors such as workload and capacity.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Apart from urgent cases that will be assigned to the PDO, we do not expect fundamental differences between the cases handled by the PDO or CLAS.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: On Mr Saktiandi Supaat's query on the exchange and sharing of knowledge between CLAS and the PDO, we will consider this at the appropriate stage and share what we can, subject to confidentiality and privilege.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Rest assured that the PDO is committed to playing a part in strengthening the expertise and knowledge of the defence bar.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This portal will also include the various avenues of legal assistance available so that applicants will not find it challenging to navigate should they require assistance.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This is part of our broader efforts to enhance access to justice.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We will also be collaborating with other agencies and stakeholders to plug the PDO into the social service ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We want to provide a more holistic support.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: To this end, we will consider Mr Raj Joshua Thomas' suggestions on working with the Police to inform accused persons about the PDO and making the application process simple and accessible.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: On this note, we assure Mr Lim Biow Chuan that there are rules governing the conduct of our Police officers when dealing with any witness, suspect or accused person.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: If Mr Lim feels that any information given by any Police officer to an accused person is improper, he may wish to share this with the relevant authorities so that they can look into it.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I also thank Mr Saktiandi for his suggestion for a one-stop shop to apply for all types of legal aid.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We can consider this as part of our broader efforts to shape the access to justice ecosystem in the future.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The PDO is a significant move that will benefit society and enhance access to justice.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We are establishing the PDO to institutionalise public defence.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We will continue to work closely with all our partners and stakeholders to ensure that criminal defence aid goes to those who need it most, when they need it most.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The trouble I had was that there was no such definition in the Bill itself.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And the phrase "criminal proceedings" was also not defined.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: With that, I seek leave to withdraw my amendment.

speaker: The Chairman
text: And you are seeking leave to withdraw the amendment?
